sec.p: The preanalyzed data used for this preliminary selection of markers are available and have been described (Kubiś and Figiel, 2023).

sec.title: scRNA-seq
sec.p: We performed scRNA-seq using cells from 60-day-old entire fused brain organoids or from E13.5 mouse embryonic brains dissected into dorsal (containing embryonic CTX, HIP, ChP) and ventral (containing embryonic STR, HYP, TH) parts.

In the case of organoids, our experimental setup included wild-type (WT) fused organoids 17D/17V (n = 3) and 21D/21V (n = 3); HD fused organoids 71D/71V (N = 3) and 77D/77V (N = 3); and mosaic HD and WT fused organoids 71D/21V (N = 3) and 21D/71V (N = 3).

In the case of our HD brain embryonic model, we used 3 mouse genotypes: WT Bac21/null, Yac128/null (containing human HTT mutant allele), Hu128/21 (containing both mutant and WT human alleles. For each mouse genotype, we collected 1 embryonic brains (total n = 3) and further divided each brain into dorsal and ventral regions, yielding 6 independent final samples, which were subjected to scRNAseq. Summarising the scRNAseq from embryonic brains was performed from dorsal region samples Bac21/null (n = 1), Hu128/21 ( n = 1), and Yac128/21 (n = 1), and the ventral region samples Bac21/null (n = 1), Hu128/21 (n = 1), and Yac128/21 (n = 1).
In total, we prepared 18 libraries for organoid-derived cells and 6 libraries for embryonic mouse brains (Fig. 1).

The day 60 organoids and dissected dorsal and ventral embryonic brains were incubated with 0.5 ml TrypLE (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 5 minutes at 37°C with agitation (orbital shaker; 60 RPM), followed by gentle pipette trituration, further incubation for 3 minutes, followed by another 10 times gentle trituration. TrypLE was inactivated by diluting the sample with 1 mL of PBS-EDTA containing 0.01% BSA, then centrifuging for 3 min at 300 x g. The cells were resuspended in 1 ml of PBS-EDTA with 0.01% BSA, with few pipetting actions, and passed through a 40 µm cell strainer. The cell number was determined using Trypan Blue and manual counting under a light microscope. A suspension of 300.000 cells/mL was prepared from the initial cell suspension using PBS-EDTA with 0.01% BSA.

Encapsulation of cells and further processing were prepared according to the protocol outlined in the Nadia source publication (Davey et al., 2021). In brief, the cell suspension (75,000 cells) was encapsulated with barcoded beads (150,000 beads) using the Nadia Instrument (DO BIO, UK) and disposable microfluidic cartridges, according to the pre- programmed drop-seq protocol available on the instrument. The droplet beads underwent multiple purification steps using Überstrainer and were washed with 6 x SSC, Tris-EDTA (TE), and Tween solutions to remove the oil remnants from the beads. Subsequently, the beads with captured RNA were reverse transcribed (Maxima RT Fisher Scientific, incubation 30 min RT + 90min 42°C), and the unused barcodes were removed from the beads with exonuclease I (NEB, incubation 45min 37°C), according to the Nadia protocol (Davey et al., 2021). For 3’ mRNA profiling, cDNA libraries were amplified using a PCR reaction (2,000 beads per reaction) with Kapa HiFi Mix (Roche) and Smart PCR Primer, employing the previously described protocol (Davey et al., 2021) and (Macosko et al., 2015) with modifications of the PCR cycle extending up to 15 cycles. The amplified cDNA was purified using Ampure XP beads, and concentrations were estimated using the Qubit assay. Subsequently, libraries for sequencing (NextSeq550 platform) were prepared using the Nextera XT/Vazyme kits and protocols (Illumina/Vazyme), which was modified after the tagmentation step by adding number of cycles up to 18. For library amplification, custom Index2 (I5) was used to select only tagmentation products that included UMI and BARCODE sequences (Davey et al., 2021; Macosko et al., 2015). The library size was adjusted with Ampur XP beads, and its quality and quantity was checked using a quantity control via the Qubit assay and a quality control via the TapeStation System. Sequencing was performed on the Illumina NextSeq550 platform using the NextSeq 500/550 High Output Kit v2.5 (150 Cycles). The sequencing depth was adjusted to around 10,000 reads per cell, which is sufficient for general single-cell characteristics concerning the count of organoids and mouse embryonic brains sequenced.

sec.title: Bioinformatic Analysis of scRNA-seq data for rare cell populations
sec.p: Raw FASTQ reads collected from the NextSeq 550 were analyzed using the JSEQ_scRNAseq v.2.3.2 bioinformatics pipeline. The pipeline was previously described (Kubiś and Figiel, 2023) and is available at https://github.com/jkubis96/JSEQ_scRNAseq.

In brief, the analysis in the pipeline included read quality control (FASTP) and annotation to the human GRCh38.p13 genome for organoid data, whereas for mouse embryonic brains, the data were annotated to the GRCm38.p6 mouse genome. Further pipeline steps included UMI and BARCODES quality control and repair (UMI-tools, DropSeq), data clustering with marker selection (Seurat), and other additional steps previously described in detail (Kubiś and Figiel, 2023) for the final production of high-resolution data, including rare cell populations occurring in organoids and embryonic brains. The cell populations were also annotated for their biological functions. Analyses were conducted with default settings included in the JSEQ_scRNAseq pipeline and described in the manual available on GitHub and in the publication.

Data from biological replicates were integrated within each genotype, but analyzed separately across distinct genotypes (e.g., 17D/17V, 21D/71V, 71D/71V, or embryos, e.g., HU128/21). This genotype-specific approach yielded higher resolution data, allowing for the precise mapping of cellular subtypes (via JSEQ_scRNAseq) to broader regional populations (e.g., CTX, STR, Ch) and enabling the identification of the ChP population. While our final analyses focus on these major cell types rather than their specific subtypes (in accordance with reviewer feedback), this high-resolution step was essential for the accurate annotation and interpretation of the complete dataset.

Downstream analyses, including data integration across genotypes (which were previously analyzed separately via JSEQ_cssg to preserve high clustering resolution - cell subtypes according to JSEQ_scRNAseq documentation), were performed using the JDtI Python library v0.2.7 (https://github.com/jkubis96/JDtI). Organoid and embryonic brain datasets were integrated independently. Cells with an unknown lineage were excluded from the analysis. During integration, the high-resolution cell subtypes identified in JSEQ_scRNAseq were merged into main cellular populations (STR, CTX, HIP, TET, ChP, MGE, CGE, LGE) to highlight broader developmental changes across these main populations.

In the JDtI workflow, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was conducted using the top marker genes for each cell population (top 20 for organoids and top 50 for embryonic brains). These markers were selected based on a Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value < 0.05 and log(FC) > 0, and were sorted primarily by Cohen’s d effect size, followed by decreasing log(FC). Using the top 25 principal components (PCs), the data were harmonized using the Harmony algorithm incorporated within JDtI. This was followed by a semi-supervised UMAP dimensionality reduction that incorporated cell population metadata. For comparison, unharmonized data and unsupervised UMAP representations are provided in the supplementary materials. UMAP parameters were set to min_dist = 0.01, n_neighbors = 15, using the Euclidean distance metric. Average gene expression was visualized using dot plots, where both dot size and color intensity reflect the average expression within a given cell population, with additional labels indicating dataset origin.

sec.title: Identification of the differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and ORA processes
sec.p: Initially, scRNA-seq transcriptomes were pooled by genotype to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs). For organoid models, comparisons were made between HD (71D/71V and 77D/77V) and controls (17D/17V and 21D/21V), as well as between mosaic and control samples. For embryonic brains, comparisons included YAC128Q/null versus BAC21Q/null, and Hu128Q/21Q versus BAC21Q/null. This differential expression analysis was performed using the JDtI Python library (v0.2.7). Significant DEGs were selected based on a Mann-Whitney U test p-value ≤ 0.05 and a minimum log(FC) ≥ 0.5, and were visualized using volcano plots to compare disease versus healthy datasets.

The identified DEGs were subsequently subjected to over-representation analysis (ORA) using the GEDSpy v.2.1.3 Python library with default settings (https://github.com/jkubis96/GEDSpy). Enrichment analysis was performed for Gene Ontology (GO) terms and biological pathways (REACTOME, KEGG) utilizing a Fisher’s exact test. P-values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) method, and only terms with an adjusted p-value ≤ 0.05 were considered significant. This analysis was conducted separately for up- and down-regulated gene pools.

To identify biological terms that were differentially enriched between the up- and down- regulated gene sets, we calculated a specific ’term fold change’. This metric normalizes gene occurrence and was defined as the number of term-associated genes divided by the total number of input genes in the respective pool. Using a cutoff of fold change ≥ 1.5, the qualifying terms were manually curated to retain only those associated with altered development, which were then assigned to arbitrary functional groups. These development-related core terms, initially identified from the HD and control organoid DEGs, were subsequently applied to downstream analyses of mosaic organoids and embryonic brains. The complete GEDSpy analysis output is available in the supplementary data.

sec.title: RNA Isolation and RT-qPCR
sec.p: After medium removal, HD forebrain organoids were washed once with PBS, transferred to 1,5 mL Eppendorf tubes, and then covered with 1 mL of TRIzol reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instruction and frozen in -80°C. Upon thaw, total RNA isolation was performed according to the manufacturer’s protocol with chloroform, isopropanol, 75% ethanol, and RNase-free water. Reverse transcription was performed using Maxima H Minus Reverse Transcriptase (Thermo Fisher) (200U per reaction) on 1 µg of RNA in 20 µl of total reaction according to the manufacturer’s protocol. For priming a mixture of random hexamers (25 pmol) and oligo(dT) 18 (25 pmol) was used. Additionally, RiboLock RNase inhibitor was added to the reaction mix (20U). Before adding the enzyme and the inhibitor, templates were denatured in 65°C for 5 minutes; after mixing all reaction reagents, the reaction was incubated for 10 min at 25°C followed by 15 min at 50°C. The resulting cDNA was further diluted to a final concentration of 10 ng/uL and stored in -20°C. qPCR was performed on CFX96 Real-Time System (Bio-Rad) using HOT FIREPol® EvaGreen® qPCR Mix Plus (ROX) (SOLIS BIODYNE) on 1 µl of cDNA in 10 µl of total reaction volume. The reaction mix included 250/125 nM primers. All primers are listed in Table 1. Thermocycling parameters were as follows: 15 min of initial denaturation at 95°C and 39 two-step cycles with 15 s denaturation at 95°C and 60 s annealing at 60°C, followed by 5 s melt curve from 65 to 95°C, increment 0,5°C. The reaction was run on CFX96 instrument (Bio-Rad). The data were analyzed, and Cq values were determined using a regression model by CFX Manager 3.1 (Bio-Rad). ACTβ was used as a reference gene.

sec.title: Immunohistochemistry
sec.p: After medium removal, organoids were washed with PBS and fixed in cold 4% (vol/vol) paraformaldehyde (PFA) overnight at 4oC. Then, organoids were stained with Ponceau S for 20 minutes, incubated in 30% sucrose solution for 24-48 hours to protect from tissue damage during freezing, and flash-frozen in OCT CompoundTM using dry ice. Flash-frozen organoids were stored in -80°C. Organoids were sectioned using Microtome cryostat (Leica) at -20°C. 25 μm sections were collected at adhesive Superfrost PlusTM glass slides and air-dried at room temperature overnight. Then, the sections were blocked in 4% Normal Goat Serum (NGS) in TBS-T buffer for 1 h at room temperature. Primary antibodies were diluted in solution 4% NGS in TBS-T. All of primary antibodies used in this study are listed in Table 2. Secondary antibodies were used in 1:500 dilution in 4% NGS in TBS-T. Hoechst 33258 was used to visualize nuclei. A series of fluorescent confocal pictures of human brain organoids were acquired using either the TCS SP5 II (Leica Microsystems; Poland) or Opera Phoenix Plus High-Content Screening System with x40 magnification, which required assembling images along the x-, y-, and z-axis. After using the Opera Screening System, the assembly operation was conducted using JIMG v.2.1.9., available at https://github.com/jkubis96/JIMG.

sec.title: Western Blot Analysis
sec.p: Fused organoids were harvested from 60-days old cultures. Blood samples were harvested from 6-8-month-old Yac128Q/null and Bac21Q/null mice. All tissues were homogenized in a phosphate buffer (0.1M, pH 7.5) with 2 mM PMSF using pipetting, followed by bath sonication for 10 min. The protein concentration was estimated using a Pierce BCA protein assay kit (Thermo Scientific, Rockford, IL, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. For each analysis, 20 ug of total protein was diluted in a loading buffer containing 2-mercaptoethanol and boiled for 5 min. The proteins were separated by SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (4–15% Mini-PROTEAN® TGX™ Precast Protein Gels, BIO-RAD), transferred to nitrocellulose, and stained with Ponceau S solution. The blots were blocked with 5% non-fat milk in PBS/0.05% Tween 20 for 1 h at RT and, subsequently, incubated for 24 h at 4°C with the primary antibodies listed in Table 2. Lamin B1 (Proteintech) protein or bands detected after Ponceau S solution staining were used as a reference for normalization of the TTR monomer (Proteintech) or TTR tetramer (DSHB) levels in blood serum, respectively. For TTR monomer detection, the blots were probed with the respective HRP-conjugated secondary antibody (anti-rabbit or anti-mouse, 1:5000; Jackson ImmunoResearch, Suffolk, UK). The immunoreaction was detected using the ECL substrate (ThermoFisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). For fluorescent Western blot analysis, a secondary antibody directed against mouse IgG, labeled with the Alexa Fluor 488 (Jackson ImmunoResearch; 1:1000) was used.

sec.title: Statistics
sec.p: Statistics were performed using GraphPad Prism 5 (version 5.00), JAMOVI 2.7.30, and R v. 4.1.2 in RStudio. In GraphPad, statistical analyses for Western blots and some qPCR analyses were conducted using t-tests to compare a single variable. In R software, analyses for qPCR and organoid size were performed. After the Levene test showed equal variance, one-way ANOVA was used for multi-group analysis, followed by post hoc t-tests (qPCR without p-value adjustment; organoid size with Bonferroni adjustment). If variance was unequal, Welch’s ANOVA was used, followed by post hoc Welch’s t-tests (qPCR without p-value adjustment; organoid size with Bonferroni adjustment). Statistical Modeling and Variance Framework.

For conditioning data, the linear mixed-effects model (LMM) was generated by JAMOVI 2.7.30 and R. Multiple organoid types were cultivated simultaneously and subjected to conditioned-medium cross-supplementation; therefore, they were analyzed as a single dataset (n = 78) to evaluate the paracrine effects and shared experimental timeframe. The LMM incorporated organoid group, conditioning, culture day, and higher-order interaction terms (group x conditioning x culture day), as fixed effects. To properly account for the longitudinal nature of the data and the correlation among repeated measurements within the same culture wells (following spontaneous aggregation into n=2), cumulative area [mm2] was measured, and individual culture wells were modeled as a random intercept. We calculated degrees of freedom and fixed-effects p-values using the Satterthwaite approximation. Group-specific estimated marginal means and 95% Wald confidence intervals were obtained directly from this combined variance. Following the multi-way ANOVA and omnibus tests of fixed effects, we performed simple slope analyses to determine the precise growth speed (in mm2 per day) for each genotype and conditioning combination across time. Simple slopes, along with their corresponding standard errors, t- statistics, and p-values, were derived directly from our LMM and the interaction.

body.p: This manuscript employs dorsal-ventral telencephalic organoids derived from Huntington's disease (HD) patient iPSCs, together with analyses of HD mouse embryos, to investigate early neurodevelopmental alterations associated with juvenile HD. This invaluable study addresses an important and emerging aspect of HD biology, namely the contribution of developmental defects to disease pathogenesis, and provides solid evidence for altered differentiation trajectories and cell fate specification. The data supports the conclusion that HD cells exhibit abnormal neurodevelopmental programs, including an increased propensity to acquire choroid plexus identity, thereby implicating developmental dysregulation as a potential contributor to HD pathogenesis.
[Editor's note: This version has been assessed by the Reviewing Editor without further input from the original reviewers.]

In the manuscript "Identification of neurodevelopmental organization of the cell populations of Juvenile Huntington's disease using dorso-ventral HD organoids and HD mouse embryos," the authors establish a fused dorso-ventral system that mimics cortex-striatum interactions within a single organoid and use this system to investigate neurodevelopmental impairments caused by HD. Specifically, they describe certain phenotypes in 60-day HD organoids and the brains of humanized mouse embryos, utilizing both wet-lab and single-cell sequencing techniques. The authors also develop dorsal/ventral and ventral/dorsal mosaic control/HD organoids, showing a capacity to rescue some HD phenotypes.
After revision the manuscript is a valuable contribution to the field.

The article titled "Identification of neurodevelopmental organization of the cell populations of juvenile Huntington's disease using dorso-ventral HD organoids and HD mouse embryos" analyses an in vitro human brain organoid model containing dorsal and ventral telencephalum structures derived from human iPSC from Huntington's disease patients or control subjects.

The authors describe differences in the pattern of expression of genes related to proliferation and neuronal maturation, with a slower pattern of differentiation present in HD cells. Moreover, the authors described a higher differentiation capacity of HD cells to generate choroid plexus identity following dorsal telencephalon prime protocol differentiation when compared to control cells.
The following is the authors’ response to the original reviews.

disp-quote.p: In the manuscript "Identification of neurodevelopmental organization of the cell populations of Juvenile Huntington's disease using dorso-ventral HD organoids and HD mouse embryos," the authors establish a fused dorso-ventral system that mimics cortex-striatum interactions within a single organoid and use this system to investigate neurodevelopmental impairments caused by HD. Specifically, they describe certain phenotypes in 60-day HD organoids and the brains of humanized mouse embryos, utilizing both wet-lab and single-cell sequencing techniques. The authors also develop dorsal/ventral and ventral/dorsal mosaic control/HD organoids, showing a capacity to rescue some HD phenotypes.

The manuscript could be a valuable contribution to the field, however it has relevant drawbacks, the most significant being a lack of clarity regarding the replicates used for each genotype in the sequencing analyses. The lack of information on replicates raises the possibility that only a single replicate was analyzed for each organoid and brain sample. This approach may lead to concerns regarding the reproducibility of the findings, and it may be necessary for the authors to generate additional data to strengthen their conclusions. In addition, the analysis of the HD samples was conducted by pooling distinct cell populations from different brain regions (CTX, HIP, ChP for the dorsal brain, and STR, HYP, TH for the ventral brain). It is unclear why scRNA seq was used on pooled brain regions, which could obscure region-specific insights.

body.p: The information we provided in the manuscript should include more details for a proper assessment of the experimental flow, replicates, and other aspects. The lack of clarity was partly due to the multivariate nature of our experimental system. For example, for scRNA-seq, there were 24 experiments, and we apologize for not including that information. The response to the “Major points” section of this review now offers a detailed description of the setup and a thorough clarification of the replicates. We also introduce a new schematic figure to help clarify the experimental setup and replicates. Additionally, all figure legends have been thoroughly rewritten, and many other changes have been made to better highlight the experimental replicates.

disp-quote.p: Another issue pertains to their proposed outcome: "Finally, we found that TTR protein, a choroid plexus marker, is elevated in the adult HD mouse serum, indicating that TTR may be a promising marker for detecting HD". This statement appears to lack statistical support, which makes this set of data potentially misleading and inconclusive.

body.p: We strongly agree that the sentence was inconclusive, and we have now corrected the Figure 11 legend and rewritten the parts of the Discussion and conclusions. We also agree that further studies with a larger number of subjects, investigating a broader age range and using more sensitive methods, such as SIMOA, are necessary to better characterize changes in TTR levels in serum.

disp-quote.p: The authors are encouraged to provide evidence of biological replicates, remove outcomes that lack statistical support, and address a series of points as detailed elsewhere.

body.p: Thank you for your thorough and valuable feedback, highlighting the important points. We address the specific points in detail below.

disp-quote.p: Major Points:

(1) In paragraphs 2.4 and 2.5, the authors describe the single-cell sequencing experiment without specifying replicates. If only a single replicate per genotype was sequenced, these analyses should be presented as preliminary and descriptive, with conclusions accordingly tempered.

body.p: As stated in our earlier responses, we acknowledge that the information provided in the manuscript is insufficient for properly assessing experimental replicates and other details. Below is our detailed explanation:
In our work, we performed 24 independent scRNAseq experiments in total:
- BAC21/null dorsal n = 1
- HU128/21 dorsal n = 1
- YAC128/null dorsal n = 1
- BAC21/null ventral n = 1
- HU128/21 ventral n = 1
- YAC128/null ventral n = 1
(1) The experimental setup of scRNAseq of 60-day-old HD, and control organoids:

We performed 18 scRNA-seq experiments, consisting of 6 organoid types with 3 replicates each. Specifically, we used two types of control fused dorso-ventral organoids: 17Q/17Q with n = 3 and 21Q/21Q with n = 3, two types of HD fused dorso-ventral organoids: 71Q/71Q with n = 3 and 77Q/77Q with n = 3, and two types of mosaic HD-control fused dorso-ventral organoids: 21Q/71Q with n = 3 and 71Q/21Q with n = 3.
(2) The experimental setup of scRNAseq of HD model embryonic brains:

We performed scRNA-seq, using 3 mouse embryonic brains divided into 3 dorsal and 3 ventral brain parts originating from manual dissection of 1 embryos of each genotype. This resulted in a total of 6 independent scRNA-seq samples, specifically: BAC21/null dorsal n = 1, BAC21/null ventral n = 1, YAC128/null dorsal n = 1, YAC128/null ventral n = 1, Hu128/21 dorsal n = 1, and Hu128/21 ventral n = 1.
Regarding the possible confusion about embryonic brain region dissection and pooling:

We collected dorsal and ventral E13.5 embryonic brain parts, assuming they included specific embryonic brain regions. For example, we believed that the hippocampus (HIP) and the choroid plexus (ChP) were collected with the cortex (CTX) as parts of the dorsal region. Similarly, the striatum (STR) was collected with the ventral brain region representing the developing future basal ganglia. This approach of collecting the regions together was necessary because most parts of the E13.5 brains are still in the primordium stage; therefore, manual separation of regions is not feasible. However, it is possible to define populations using RNAseq, which we confirmed in our experiments.
We now have also included the control analysis of our dissection accuracy in the Results section 2.10:

“First, we evaluated the transcriptomes of cell populations from the ventral compartment to assess the robustness of segregation of subpallial structures and to rule out technical artifacts arising from dissection of the ventral and dorsal parts of embryonic brains (Fig. 9). The cell populations from control BAC21/null embryos recapitulated canonical gradients of Foxp1 and Foxp2 across the ganglionic eminences (Ferland et al., 2003; Takahashi et al., 2003). The LGE showed strong Foxp2 expression levels but lacked Foxp1, while the MGE displayed the opposite pattern, with high Foxp1 levels. The CGE populations had an intermediate profile, predominantly expressing Foxp2 with moderate Foxp1. In the STR cluster, both Foxp1 and Foxp2 were consistently expressed across HD and controls, though Foxp1 was slightly reduced in the heterozygous HU128/21 embryo. This consistent spatial pattern of core striatal and subpallial populations after scRNAseq suggests that our tissue dissection was very precise and that our dataset offers high resolution.”
Therefore, our 6 scRNA-seq experiments are a valuable, high-resolution and exact representation of the cell composition of the mouse embryonic brain.
To improve the understanding of our experiments, we now provide:
(1) Figure 1 to more clearly illustrate our manuscript across all experiments, including the number of replicates.
(2) A thorough revision of the manuscript detailing the sample preparation and number, including the scRNA-seq experiment.
(3) Enhanced descriptions of Figures with detailed explanations, sample numbers, and statistics.

disp-quote.p: (2) Text seems poorly assembled in some parts and experiments lack proper introduction. For example in paragraph 2.2, portions like "Our qPCR (Supplement 1A) and RNA-seq DEG results detected [...]" (line 149) and "[...] which is consistent with the results from GSEA (Supp. Fig. 2A; Supp. 1)" (line 164) seem out of place, as qPCR and RNA-seq generation or GSEA analysis were not previously introduced in the main text.

body.p: We revised these sections carefully to ensure proper text assembly, improve the description, and provide an introduction to the experiments.

disp-quote.p: (3) In Suppl. Fig. 1A, the dorsal marker TBR1 and the ventral marker GSX2 in CTRL organoids, as well as the ventral markers DLX2 and NKX2.1 in HD organoids, show similar expression between dorsal and ventral regions. This is unexpected.

body.p: Figure 2 (now main figure set) shows the results of characterizing the organoids using a common set of markers. Although this marker set is widely accepted in developmental studies, it remains a somewhat coarse method for distinguishing different cell stages. While these markers are frequently used in organoid research, they are highly sensitive to even minor variations in organoid development. Currently, our understanding of these markers' functions is better than when they were first incorporated into characterization protocols. For instance, DLX2 plays a crucial role in determining the fate of neuronal and oligodendrocytic cells, as well as in the development of soft facial tissue. In contrast, GSX2 promotes neurogenesis while inhibiting oligodendroglia. Therefore, although both are ventral markers, their functions differ considerably in regulating ventral region development. Variability in the expression of dorsal and ventral markers may be influenced by notable heterogeneity in the organoid formation process, despite careful control. Additionally, the heterogeneity and detailed expression levels have been only sparsely studied in HD organoids, resulting in a lack of comprehensive reference data.

disp-quote.p: (4) The authors should better characterize the ventral and cortical identities in both CTRL and HD organoids to clarify whether HD organoids correctly differentiate (in terms of typical dorsal and ventral markers) relative to CTRL organoids. This information is particularly relevant in light of subsequent analyses of WT-HD mosaic organoids.

body.p: A large portion of our work already involves characterizing HD and control organoids on many levels, as well as investigating how HD brain development differs from that of a normal brain in the organoid model. Hence, the simplified question addressed in this work is whether HD organoids correctly differentiate. Unfortunately, as we mentioned earlier, extensive characterization of the organoids using typical markers (via imaging or mRNA analysis) and as single dorsal or ventral organoids does not provide the accuracy needed to draw firm conclusions about the differentiation profile. This is because the abnormal features of HD organoid differentiation, such as the presence of certain cell populations and an increased number of rosettes, were not previously recognized in the early stage of organoid differentiation. In addition, as we demonstrate, the differentiation to brain-like structures in HD organoids is greatly influenced by the fusion of dorsal and ventral primed organoids. To achieve greater precision in investigating the differentiation of HD organoids, we systematically identified cell populations, their markers, and GSEA results across all setups using an advanced organoid characterization method, scRMAseq. To compare how our organoids differentiate, we used an HD mouse brain, where separating into the ventral and dorsal regions is mechanically feasible. This confirmed that similar HD-related processes occur in organoids and brain tissue models.

disp-quote.p: (5) Data in Fig. 4 are misleading. In particular:
The authors find an upregulation of LIMK2 in HD organoids compared with 21Q CTRL organoids, but not with 33Q CTRL organoids. How do they interpret this result?

body.p: The 33Q organoids are derived from iPSCs of individuals who carry the HTT gene with 33 CAGs. This count exceeds the average found in healthy patients. A CAG range between 36 and 39 is considered to exhibit reduced penetrance, while 33 CAGs (27-35 CAGs) is sometimes regarded as placing an individual "at risk" (intermediate) or at risk of transmission to offspring. Our results clearly indicate that this clinical assessment is justified and that the 33Q organoids may show some distinct features of HD organoids, revealing early markers that affect disease progression. However, we do not have a definitive explanation of the observed phenomenon.

disp-quote.p: How do they explain that other inhibitory neuron markers show opposite or inconsistent trends compared with LIMK2?

body.p: The Limk2 belongs to the major regulatory network of transcriptionally deregulated genes in HD governed by the SMAD3 pathway. Interestingly, Limk2 within this regulatory network shows upregulated expression in HD models. At the same time, the majority of other genes in this network are downregulated, thus exhibiting the opposite pattern (10.15252/msb.20167435). The possible explanation is that the Limk2 gene is associated with the early organization of inhibitory neuron fate, specifically in astral microtubule organization and mitotic spindle orientation during the early stages of mitosis. In contrast, the other markers we investigated are linked to more advanced neuronal development and maturation stages. Our transcriptional results, including Limk2, indicate a prevalence of early development in HD organoids, while lower expression of late markers suggests reduced maturation in HD organoids. This observation is in line with our key finding that early development of the HD brain is delayed at the level of organoids and embryonic mouse model brain.

disp-quote.p: The authors describe upregulation of GPR88 and HS3ST4 in HD organoids (77Q), but this data lacks statistical support.
The authors state that CCL2 is downregulated in 71Q and 77Q organoids; however, the graph and statistics indicate the opposite result.

body.p: Thank you for carefully reading and identifying inconsistencies in the manuscript. We want to clarify that these are unintended errors that occurred during repeated proofreading of the statistical tests used. Although the analyses are correct in the figure, they are not correct in the results text. The text is now corrected in the new version of the manuscript text.

disp-quote.p: (6) Cell Number Balance: the cell count per sample (and thus per genotype, given the probable lack of replicates) is highly unbalanced, ranging from ~500 for 17Q/17Q to ~5000 for 71Q/71Q (Supp. Figures 4 and 5). This imbalance strongly impacts the number of identified cell subtypes. The authors should consider down-sampling cells across genotypes to match the minimum cell count for any genotype, and then report the resulting number of cell types.

body.p: These differences in the number of cells for each genotype are closely related to the cell phenotypes observed during the harvesting, dissociation, and encapsulation processes, which varied among organoid genotypes. We obtained more consistent cell numbers for embryos, where each genotype was clonal with the same background. Some of these challenges could not be avoided, so we decided to utilize the analytical approach presented in our publication. We agree that the number of input cells can lead to the identification of more subtypes, but our previous study demonstrates that more subtypes with this analytical approach occur in highly proliferating and differentiating tissues, such as organoids (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2023.04.20.537649v1).

However, when comparing the percentages of CTX, MGE, STR, etc., we used the number of cells relative to the total cell count from datasets for this genotype (three replicates for each genotype). This approach was more balanced because it was based on the proportion of each cell type relative to the total number of cells for this genotype, rather than comparing only subtypes. Additionally, we decided to conduct a combined transcriptomic analysis to examine the main changes in developmental pathways between HD and CTRL organoids and embryonic brains, as the expression values are normalized to each cell instead of to the dataset, as in traditional RNA-seq approaches. This method allowed us to highlight the primary changes in developing CTRL and HD brains at the cell level using organoid models and mouse embryonic brains. Furthermore, we narrowed the data to elements consistent across the genotypes of CTRL organoids and similarly for HD organoids, thereby minimizing genotype-related changes in the single-cell analysis. This strategy enabled a more targeted analysis in subsequent DEG and ORA, reducing the impact of genotype-specific variations.
Summarizing, we preferred to avoid reducing the data (the number of cells) for comparison due to the potential for inaccurate data curation.

disp-quote.p: (7) Despite generating single-cell data, the authors decide to pool cells across all cell types to perform a bulk differential expression analysis. Given the nine general populations identified, differential expression results between conditions should be reported for each population.

body.p: We have decided to poll the cell transcriptomes from scRNA-seq datasets, which produce RNA-seq datasets. This is important because such RNAseq enables us to collect more information from different research perspectives, fully explore the data, and enhance comparisons of the identified cell populations.
The following important information can be collected from conducting the bulk differential expression analysis on datasets with combined cell transcriptomes.

(1) Investigating total RNA expression enables the identification of a broader set of genes that may vary to a certain degree among populations. Due to the complexity of physiological cellular networks, these genes reflect the activation of similar processes across populations, which is a necessary complement that scRNAseq cannot provide. Additionally, this analysis increases the statistical power of the study.
(2) Investigating global gene sets provides the opportunity to uncover paracrine processes that may indicate interactions among cell populations affected by mutant proteins.

(3) Finally, the RNAseq data also provides information about a set of genes reflecting the maturity and developmental advancement of our organoids and brains affected by mutant proteins, greatly supplementing the information about cell populations from scRNAseq.

disp-quote.p: (8) Improvement of UMAP Representation: The authors should enhance the clarity of UMAPs (Figures 6 and 7). For instance, they could use one panel to color cells by sample and another to show clusters of the nine main populations (if clustering was performed). Additionally, it would be beneficial to report UMAPs before using the Harmony batch integration algorithm. Lastly, pie charts could be converted to bar plots representing cell proportions, with all samples displayed side by side to facilitate comparisons.

body.p: We have now changed Figures 6 and 7, which are now Figures 8 and 9. We have prepared the figures according to the reviewer's request and updated the UMAP representations. We colored by samples and by main populations. We also report the UMAPs before Harmony in Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6 for organoids and embryo brains. The pie charts are now converted to bar plots.

disp-quote.p: (9) Figure 8 is crowded and difficult to interpret. The authors might consider using a dot plot with associated UMAPs to represent known marker expression in the nine main populations, moving the subpopulation dot plot to the Supplementary section.

body.p: We rethought Figure 8, removed the markers, and introduced a new Figure 10. The analysis in Figure 10 examines positional markers such as dorsal EMX2, FOXG1, LHX2, and TBR1, ventral markers FOXP1, FOXP2, and ETV1, and ciliary markers ARL13B and IFT88, which allow us to better illustrate the developmental defect present in HD in both organoids and the brain. Figure 10 shows that HD organoids and HD mouse brains exhibit neural positional dysorganization. In particular, it shows the MGE and ChP regions as the most affected in HD. Please see the results and discussion for details.

disp-quote.p: (10) Despite Figure 9 showing no statistically significant difference in TTR levels between WT and HD mice, the authors claim "Our findings show an increase in the level of TTR monomer (16 kDa) and tetramer (55 kDa) [...] (Figure 9)" (line 375). Since TTR is proposed as a marker based on these inconclusive data, paragraph 2.9 and the corresponding conclusions require revision.

body.p: We agree that the initial phrasing overstated the conclusion, as the necessary statistical power was not achieved in the serum analysis. The experiment is based on sera from only a few HD mice; therefore, the necessary power was not achieved. However, the intention of the sentence was not to highlight the finding in serum but rather to summarize all the evidence in the manuscript, indicating that the “TTR may be a promising marker gene.” The sentence aimed to consolidate in vivo and in vitro results, including increased levels of TTR mRNA in qPCR of HD organoids, elevated TTR in dorsal HD embryonic brain regions and organoids via scRNAseq, and a higher number of ChP cell populations in HD, along with immunofluorescence (IF) data. The serum data show similar TTR levels, supporting this hypothesis, with several mice as biological replicates, indicating the trend; however, more individual mouse sera were needed for better examination and justified statistics. Of note, the co-authors of this study have previously reported elevated levels of this marker in adult patients with CSF (DOI: 10.1093/braincomms/fcac309).

Therefore, we now mention in the text it is not significant.: We showed that the marker differed between individual YAC128/null mice and BAC21Q/null controls (Fig. 11), mainly for the Ttr tetramer. We, however, did not observe statistical significance in the mean comparisons.

disp-quote.p: (11) The initial part of the "Discussion" (lines 380-426) reads more like an "Introduction"

body.p: Thank you for this suggestion. We now optimized the text for redundancy and incorporated some information to the introduction section to provide better context and flow.

disp-quote.p: (12) The phenotypic rescue observed in WT-HD mosaic organoids is particularly intriguing with therapeutic implications for HD. This should be more thoroughly emphasized in the discussion. For example, data in Fig. 2B indicate that "On average, mosaic 21D/71V organoids were close in size to control organoids, while the opposite configuration of mosaic 71D/21V was closer to HD organoids (Fig. 2B)" (lines 143-144). Thus, they observe size rescue only in the 21D/71V mosaic configuration, not in 71D/21V. How do they interpret this finding? Additionally, when examining single-cell data in Fig. 6, they find that the ChP cell population in both WT-HD mosaic configurations (21D/71V and 71D/21V) is reduced or absent, as in control organoids, indicating that the rescue in this parameter is seen in both configurations, unlike the size parameter. The authors should discuss more thoroughly how the combination of WT and HD cells may have beneficial effects or not.

body.p: Using healthy cells to create either the dorsal or ventral side and forming mosaic organoids reverses the effects in fused organoids, where both the dorsal and ventral parts are HD.
In the discussion section, we have now introduced additional explanations:
(1) The base size of the HD organoids is increased:

HD brain organoids display more early proliferative features at the expense of differentiation compared to controls. This has been confirmed through the extended HD organoid structure, rosettes, GSEA patterns, and scRNAseq.
(2) The size rescue only in 21D/71V but not in 71D/21V mosaic organoids:

In general, there is consensus that the physiologically dorsal part of the brain proliferates at a higher rate than the ventral side during development; however, both mutant and normal HTT influence proliferation on both sides. This dorso-ventral imbalance, driven by mutant HTT in combination with the mosaic organoid setup, likely results in a much larger 71D/21V than 21D/71V.
(3) The choroid plexus population rescues in both 21D/71V and 71D/21V:

During brain development, choroid plexus cells originate from the ectoderm and mesoderm. Additionally, choroid plexus cells are known for their secretory functions and for communicating with surrounding tissues via extracellular mediators. This communication closely regulates NSC proliferation and differentiation, which may also explain size differences between organoids. Moreover, we show that HD organoids and HD mouse brains show positional dysorganisation, being between neural cells and choroid tissue, as seen in the transcriptional profile. Given all this, we cannot definitively say that the choroid plexus in HD organoids comes only from the dorsal side, since many brain regions in HD contribute to its final development due to positional defects. Therefore, both ventral and dorsal parts of the organoid are also likely involved in rescuing the HD phenotype in mosaic. Furthermore, introducing either a dorsal or a ventral healthy part can diminish the choroid plexus phenotype. Lastly, the features of the mosaic organoids (either 21D/71V or 71D/21V) also include a reduced dosage of the mutant allele within the organoid.

Notably, our mouse model setup allows us to examine the brains of HD embryos (both ventral and dorsal parts) that either contain or lack the healthy allele. Interestingly, the choroid plexus phenotype is milder in YAC128/BAC21 compared to the much more pronounced choroid plexus phenotype in YAC128/null. Therefore, the presence of the healthy allele decreases the number of choroid plexus cells compared to having only the HD allele, thus resulting in the rescue of the phenotype.

(13) Fig. 1B shows a representative slice of an HD fused organoid stained for the dorsal marker TBR1. Authors should include staining for a ventral marker as well, ideally on the same section.

disp-quote.p: (15) The authors state, "[...], we observed the regression in the HD phenotype represented by reduced neural rosette occurrence, which is consistent with the results from GSEA (Supp. Fig. 2 A; Supp. 1)" (lines 163-165). A clearer explanation of this consistency is needed.

body.p: The fragment has been revised to provide a more precise explanation of the sentence's specific points.

disp-quote.p: (16) The described Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) on DEGs to identify enriched Gene Ontology terms seems more like a Gene Ontology Enrichment analysis, as GSEA typically involves pathway-specific co-regulation analysis.

disp-quote.p: (17) The phrase "Firstly, we compared the expression of several inhibitory neuron markers" (line 179) should specify the technique used, I guess qPCR.

disp-quote.p: (19) The sentence "Such gene deregulations and GSEA profiles indicate that control organoids are more related to maturation processes than HD organoids" is unclear.

body.p: We propose to incorporate the following enhanced explanation into the manuscript content.

The statistically significant deregulated genes between HD and CTRL organoids, along with the associated biological terms and pathways related to maturation, proliferation, and differentiation, indicate that cells derived from healthy organoids are more aligned with processes involving mature glial and neuronal cells. In contrast, HD cells appear to be arrested in proliferative and differentiation stages. This is reflected in the faster development of certain brain structures in HD organoids, but with fewer processes linked to mature cells, suggesting an incomplete state of maturation.

disp-quote.p: (20) Lines 297-300 contain hypotheses that would likely fit better in the Discussion section.

body.p: The sentences were in part transferred into the discussion section.

body.p: Thank you for careful reading. The term has been revised.

disp-quote.p: (22) Why did the authors use the 71Q line instead of the 109Q line to create WT-HD mosaic organoids? In fact, the size parameter graph shows a more pronounced HD-related alteration in the 109Q line.

body.p: The reason for omitting the 109Q line was due to a specific characteristic of all HD organoids. All HD cells showed increased cell-cell adherence during dissociation attempts, making it difficult to properly prepare reproducible samples for single-cell analysis using Drop-seq technology. Unfortunately, this phenotype of cells to quickly build cellular aggregates was particularly pronounced in the 109Q cell line. Therefore, although the HD phenotype in the 109Q organoids was more pronounced (TTR, rosettes, etc.), it was very challenging and costly to perform scRNA-seq compared to 71Q and 77Q. To ensure consistency in our scRNA-seq, we decided to include only fused HD and fused mosaic samples from 71Q and 77Q.

disp-quote.p: (23) A recent publication by Galimberti et al. (Nat Comm., 2024) investigated WT-HD mosaic telencephalic organoids containing ventral and dorsal neuron populations. The authors should consider discussing their findings in relation to that work.

body.p: In the manuscript, we cite the work of Galimberti et al.

disp-quote.p: The article titled "Identification of neurodevelopmental organization of the cell populations of juvenile Huntington's disease using dorso-ventral HD organoids and HD mouse embryos" analyses an in vitro human brain organoid model containig dorsal and ventral telencephalum structures derived from human iPSC from Huntington's disease patients or control subjects.

The authors describe differences in the pattern of expression of genes related to proliferation and neuronal maturation, with a slower pattern of differentiation present in HD cells. Moreover, the authors described a higher differentiation capacity of HD cells to generate choroid plexus identity following dorsal telencephalon prime protocol differentiation when compared to control cells. Whereas the claims related to Choroid plexus identity are intriguing, most of the claims made through the manuscript are not sustained by quantitative data or consistent results in the different conditions analysed, or many experiments seem to be missing to reach final conclusions.

In addition, the quality of the organoids used for experiments does not seem to have been assessed or satisfactorily presented in the figures of this paper. Many important details related to the experimental execution are missing in the current version of this manuscript.

body.p: Thank you for your insightful feedback. We truly appreciate your thoughtful comments. In the next versions of the manuscript, we will work to address the inconsistencies and clarify the points you have raised. We will also make sure to provide more quantitative data and include any missing experiments to strengthen our conclusions. Additionally, we will pay closer attention to assessing and presenting the quality of the organoids used in the experiments and ensure that all relevant experimental details are properly included.

(2) The experimental setup of scRNAseq of HD model embryonic brains:

We performed scRNA-seq using 3 mouse embryonic brains divided into 3 dorsal and 3 ventral brain parts originating from manual dissection of 1 embryo of each genotype. Therefore, there were 6 independent scRNAseq in total, namely: BAC21/null dorsal n = 1 of BAC21/null ventral n = 1, YAC128/null dorsal n = 1, YAC128/null ventral n = 1, Hu128/21 dorsal n = 1, and Hu128/21 ventral n = 1.
Regarding the possible confusion about embryonic brain region dissection:

We collected the dorsal and ventral embryonic E13.5 brain parts, assuming they would contain certain embryonic brain regions. For example, we believed that the hippocampus (HIP) and the choroid plexus (ChP) were collected alongside the cortex (CTX) as part of the dorsal part. Similarly, the striatum (STR) was collected with the ventral brain region representing the developing future basal ganglia. Such an assumption of collecting the regions together was necessary since most of the parts of the E13.5 brains are in the stage of primordia; hence, the separation of regions is not possible manually, however, it is possible by defining populations using RNAseq, which we confirmed in our experiments.
We have now included the analysis assessing the robustness of our scRNA-seq and our dissection accuracy in the Results section 2.10:

“First, we evaluated the transcriptomes of cell populations from the ventral compartment to assess the robustness of segregation of subpallial structures and to rule out technical artifacts arising from dissection of the ventral and dorsal parts of embryonic brains (Fig. 10B). The cell populations from control BAC21/null embryos recapitulated canonical gradients of Foxp1 and Foxp2 across the ganglionic eminences (Ferland et al., 2003; Takahashi et al., 2003). The LGE showed strong Foxp2 expression levels but lacked Foxp1, while the MGE displayed the opposite pattern, with high Foxp1 levels. The CGE populations had an intermediate profile, predominantly expressing Foxp2 with moderate Foxp1. In the STR cluster, both Foxp1 and Foxp2 were consistently expressed across HD and controls, though Foxp1 was slightly reduced in the heterozygous HU128/21 embryo. This consistent spatial pattern of core striatal and subpallial populations after scRNAseq suggests that our tissue dissection was very precise and that our dataset offers high resolution.”
Therefore, our 6 scRNA-seq experiments are a valuable, high-resolution, and exact representation of the cell composition of the mouse embryonic brain.

body.p: In the present version of the manuscript, we incorporated the DAPI staining as a separate column set of picture.

The images were captured using the Opera Phenix HCS Nipcov spinning disk microscope with 5% overlap. This overlap area is common for many confocal microscopes. However, producing these images involves certain technical limitations and balances the speed of image collection, the volume of digital data, resolution, and final quality. While LSM systems are slower and provide better quality, spinning disk microscopes are very fast. Still, even with an Opera spinning disk, acquiring images takes about a day per organoid and results in terabytes of data. Stitching these images is a complex process that requires hours of processing on a powerful workstation with a dedicated program we developed. Despite this, preventing cross-shaped artifacts caused by overlapping regions, which sometimes appear in Fig. 4, is difficult. In the worst case, the entire dataset may not be stitchable, forcing us to repeat the acquisition. Currently, this presents a technical limit for the stitched images shown in the manuscript, obtained with the spinning disk Opera microscope. For more details about this imaging process, please visit our GitHub repository: https://github.com/jkubis96/JIMG.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this important observation. We would like to clarify the presentation of our ORA data in (now Supplementary Figure 1.)

The boxed titles in Supplementary Figure 1 (e.g., "Neuronal & glial cells development & maturation", "Mitotic spindle & cell polarity", "Programmed cell death") represent broad thematic meta-categories used solely to visually cluster individual Gene Ontology (GO) terms into functional domains, rather than individual biological pathways.

While both upregulated (blue) and downregulated (red) groups contain terms belonging to these overarching meta-categories, the specific individual GO terms within them reflect distinct developmental stages and opposite biological directions:
(1) Neuronal & Glial Development & Maturation:

The upregulated GO terms within this cluster correspond specifically to early progenitor processes, stem cell state maintenance, and early lineage specification (e.g., pathways regulating early neurogenesis and negative regulation of cellular differentiation).

In contrast, the downregulated GO terms correspond to late-stage structural and functional maturation (e.g., synaptic vessel transport, axonogenesis, postsynaptic assembly, and mature glial differentiation).
(2) Mitotic Spindle & Cell Polarity:
Upregulated terms center on active cell-cycle regulation, spindle assembly, and mitotic division in expanding progenitor pools.
Downregulated terms relate to structural polarity required for tissue organization, planar cell polarity in differentiating neurons, and post-mitotic structural stability.
(3) Programmed Cell Death:
Upregulated terms reflect pro-apoptotic signaling and cellular stress pathways activated during aberrant development, whereas downregulated terms involve anti-apoptotic / cell survival processes.
In the results text we incorporated a following text:

“In general, while terms enriched in both up- and downregulated datasets cluster under broad functional headers (such as 'Neuronal & glial cells development & maturation'), individual upregulated GO terms were specific to early progenitor maintenance and early differentiation steps, whereas downregulated GO terms selectively enriched for late-stage synaptic assembly, dendritic spine formation, and mature neuronal/glial function.”

body.p: We have now performed a range of new analyses of our results and a new set of experiments to test the influence of paracrine, secreted signals on the HD neurodevelopmental phenotypes. To selectively capture paracrine signals from HD or WT, we conditioned media within individual genotypes (e.g., HD media to HD organoids and WT to WT, always across V to D and D to V). Our new results are now shown in Figure 5, where we demonstrate that both dorsal and ventral sides of organoids from both wt and HD genotypes are subject to regulatory developmental paracrine influence that controls tissue growth along the striatocortical axis. The expansion of HD organoids is twice as prominent as that of WT organoids and cannot be completely halted by conditioning. This suggests that soluble paracrine signals influence the HD phenotype, but also that cell-cell contact or localized niche factors are necessary for a full rescue (two-hit mechanism).

To investigate this niche, we examined the positioning of neural cells in HD. We found ectopic expression of several positioning factors in ChP and aberrant positioning of MGE interneurons in HD. We constructed a conceptual model in which massive ChP overgrowth creates an altered paracrine environment that triggers a switch in gene expression in interneuron progenitors. The soluble secretome can modulate the proliferative tissue environment, and direct cell-cell contacts or localized extracellular matrix (ECM) niche factors are essential for preserving spatial boundaries and cell migration. This insight aligns with recent patient cohort data demonstrating structural ChP modifications and abnormal CSF dynamics prior to clinical onset.
